program_plain: World: a 64x64 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges, 8 neighbours each). Rules each step: one grain drops on a random cell; a cell reaching 4 grains topples one grain to each of its 4 neighbours (grains fall off the edge), repeated until no cell has 4 or more.

full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The rule system is the Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld (BTW) Abelian sandpile, and both observed features are documented for it.

**1. Model family.** This is statistical physics, specifically self-organized criticality (SOC). It is a slowly driven, threshold-toppling cellular automaton: one grain is added at a random site, sites topple at 4 grains, and grains are lost at the boundary. The standard names are the "BTW model" and the "Abelian sandpile model" (Dhar's name).

The description is slightly inconsistent. It mentions "wrap-around edges, 8 neighbours" but also toppling to 4 neighbours with grains falling off the edge. The toppling rule and the dissipation at the edge are what define the BTW model, so I treated it as the standard 4-neighbour open-boundary version. Wrap-around edges with no sink would not dissipate grains at all. The system size (64×64 or 128×128) only changes finite-size scales.

**2. The observed behaviour.**
- **Bursty activity.** This is the avalanche behaviour the model was built to show.
  - Bak, Tang and Wiesenfeld introduced it in "Self-organized criticality: An explanation of 1/f noise", Phys. Rev. Lett. 59, 381 (1987). Their paper described a nonlinear process with fractal characteristics and a complex, noise-like behaviour, which they claimed had a 1/f spectral density.
  - One caveat: g_activity_cv = -2.0 is odd. A coefficient of variation cannot be negative, so it may be a log-scale or normalised quantity. I could not check it against the source, and it doesn't change the verdict.
- **A dominant temporal frequency.** This is a spectral hump or peak in the activity time series at the driving rate, and it is documented. It is not an intrinsic oscillation.
  - Chhimpa & Yadav, "Avalanche activity noises in sandpile models", arXiv:2507.21484 (July 2025). It is listed on ResearchGate as published in J. Stat. Mech. in Oct 2025, but I did not confirm that on the publisher's site.
  - It finds that a finite-size BTW or Manna system has a flat low-frequency regime, a hump at intermediate frequency, and a 1/f^α power law at high frequency.
  - It interprets the peak power as a regular temporal event, namely the external drive occurring after an average time.
  - The lower cutoff and peak frequencies decay as power laws with system size.
  - That paper says an earlier work (Laurson et al.) mentioned the hump qualitatively, but without quantitative characterisation.
- **Earliest clear sources on the activity spectrum.**
  - Jensen, Christensen & Fogedby, "1/f noise, distribution of lifetimes, and a pile of sand", Phys. Rev. B 40, 7425 (1989). I verified the title, authors and journal in several search results. It states that the signal has a Lorentzian power spectrum in the BTW model.
  - Kertész & Kiss (1990), cited in the review below. It revisited BTW's question of long-time correlations by carefully analysing the power spectrum of the activity signal. I did not retrieve the original paper, so its venue and year are from memory and not verified here.
  - Later work establishes that for small systems or slow driving the activity spectrum is ~1/f² (Lorentzian). For small system sizes the spectral exponent is α ≈ 2, a Lorentzian form.
  - Laurson et al. (large-scale simulations) found an exponent significantly below 2, i.e. nontrivial 1/f^α. I only saw this second-hand, so I did not verify the paper.
- **Review.** Pradhan, "Time-Dependent Properties of Sandpiles", Frontiers in Physics 9:641233 (2021). It concludes that sandpiles generate 1/f spectra under suitable driving, but usually 1/f² spectra in the slow-driving limit.

**3. Differences and caveats.**
- The "dominant frequency" is the drive-timescale hump, or the Lorentzian corner set by the avalanche duration. If the simulation measured a sharp, system-independent peak, check whether it sits at the drive period or at a 1/(avalanche-duration) corner.
- Because the drive is one grain per step, an avalanche's duration is much longer than one step, so a peak at 1/T_drive is not necessarily a true oscillation. If the spectral peak statistic is just a max over a Lorentzian, it is a generic outcome.
- Related literature on genuine cycles is different. Shapoval et al. (Sci. Rep. 2021; PubMed 39160903, Chaos 2024) argue that stress accumulation in the slow time cycles, ending in an abrupt release. This could also produce low-frequency spectral structure, and it is a relevant relative. Authors, year and venue for this item were not fully verified. The PubMed listing is the 2024 "Explanation of flicker noise…" paper.

**4. Confidence: medium-high.**
- The identification of the model is certain.
- Bursty activity is core, well-established SOC behaviour.
- The spectral peak is documented at the level of a hump near the drive scale (Chhimpa & Yadav 2025). The spectrum shape is well characterised across BTW studies.
- I could not read most of the original 1987–1990 papers in full, so some details are second-hand. The activity-CV value and the exact nature of the spectral peak in the simulation are not checked against the literature.

**Searches run:**
- BTW SOC power spectrum 1/f noise
- sandpile activity power spectrum Lorentzian 1/f² (Jensen, Christensen, Fogedby)
- abelian sandpile periodic oscillation spectral peak finite size
- "Time-Dependent Properties of Sandpiles" authors
- Chhimpa Yadav hump power spectrum
